messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nabil is a 56-year-old married man who works as a social media manager for a regional restaurant group, spending most days monitoring feeds, drafting posts, and responding quickly to public comments. He traces the start of his current difficulties to an encounter with police outside a downtown protest nearly a year ago. He had not gone looking for trouble; he had stayed after work to meet a friend for coffee and was caught in the churn of people being pushed off the street. He remembers officers shouting contradictory commands, the crush of bodies, and being driven face-first against the hood of a car while someone forced his jaw open as he gasped for air. What still comes back most sharply is the metallic taste in his mouth—blood and pepper spray mingled together—so vividly that when the memory breaks through he can taste it again. In those moments he is flooded with rage. He also cannot bear to stay with the memory for long, cutting it off before he can recall it fully, as if letting it continue would make the whole scene happen again.

In the weeks afterward, Nabil became preoccupied with what the incident meant. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, especially those in authority, and that the world was fundamentally dangerous in ways he had once tried to deny. What cut deepest was his conviction that he had acted against his own values. He had yelled back, cursed, and in his panic shoved another man who was trying to steady himself nearby; afterward he fixated on that moment with shame, telling himself he had become someone he did not respect. From these conclusions, his habits began to narrow. Because he felt that danger could come from ordinary places and hidden intentions, he started avoiding television, films, news clips, and articles about protests or police encounters. He withdrew from anything emotionally stirring more generally, not only upsetting material but even family celebrations or sentimental movies, because strong feelings of any kind seemed capable of opening something he no longer trusted himself to manage.

That same sense of violation and danger left him living as though threat were always close. Even in his own home he could not fully relax; his shoulders stayed tight and he found himself listening for movement outside. At restaurants, in stores, in his office building, he scanned entrances, watched people’s hands, and would not settle until he had identified how to get out quickly. He was certain that vigilance was the only reasonable response in a world where appearances could not be trusted. At work this became especially concrete: when reviewing trending content he now keeps one browser tab minimized and positioned near the exit of his open-plan office, sitting where he can see who approaches from behind. If a video thumbnail shows flashing patrol lights or a crowd scene, his body reacts before he can think. The taste returns to his mouth, anger surges, and he feels a jolt of fear and horror that leaves him restless for hours, unable to come down even when he knows he is physically safe.

As these reactions intensified, they fed back into what he believed. The fact that he could not relax in harmless settings seemed to prove to him that the world really was dangerous. His constant route-checking and scanning did not feel excessive to him; they felt like evidence that he had finally seen reality clearly. And each time he noticed how quickly rage could overtake him, he took it as further proof that the encounter had changed him into someone less decent, less restrained.

Over months, Nabil’s efforts to control this became more rigid. He stopped watching television with his wife because he could not tolerate unexpected footage or even emotionally charged scenes. He curbed dinners out unless he could choose the table and map the exits first. He tries to flatten his whole inner life, avoiding not just distress but joy, tenderness, and excitement, because any feeling seems too close to the ones he dreads. Yet this emotional shutting-down has not quieted the memory. If anything, pushing it away before it is complete leaves it jagged and unfinished, returning in sensory fragments—the taste, the pressure, the flash of rage—without context or resolution. Afterward he is more watchful than ever, and more convinced that people conceal danger and that he failed some basic test of character that day.

His wife urged him to seek help after he left a family gathering abruptly, insisting on checking side doors and pacing outside because he could not calm himself. Nabil comes to treatment exhausted by the effort of staying on guard and by how small his life has become. What frightens him most is not only that the world is unsafe, but that he may never again trust his own reactions. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to sit with his wife in an ordinary room and feel like he is actually there instead of bracing for the next blow.
